nature-es-057.title: Remote sensing: watching Earth from above
nature-es-057.text: Since 1988 Brazil's space research institute has measured Amazon deforestation every year from satellite images. That is remote sensing: gathering information about an object or area from a distance, without touching it, usually by observing Earth from satellites or aircraft. Most people use it daily without noticing, in the satellite views of online maps and the cloud pictures of weather forecasts. Satellite remote sensing began with Sputnik 1 in 1957. Multispectral satellites such as Landsat, which record several bands of light, have flown since the early 1970s. The method reaches dangerous or remote places and can replace slower, costlier fieldwork without disturbing the site. Its uses run from managing forests, water and minerals to mapping wildlife habitat to monitoring greenhouse gases and detecting oil spills. Much of the water balance can be measured this way, including soil moisture, precipitation, evapotranspiration and snow. For ecosystem services, it can track the health and extent of the ground cover that provides them, helping planning and monitoring.

nature-es-051.title: GIS: linking the world's data by location
nature-es-051.text: A soil survey, a census and a map of rivers seem to have little in common. Put them in a geographic information system and they share one key: location. A GIS is a combination of computer hardware and software that stores, manages, analyzes, edits and displays geographic data. It uses location the way a database uses a shared key to link tables. At its core sits a database holding the shape and position of geographic things along with their attributes. Roger Tomlinson coined the phrase in the mid-1960s, though many of the methods GIS automates are much older. Data enter by direct measurement such as remote sensing or GPS, by digitizing paper maps, or by copying existing GIS data. Feeding in satellite data lets researchers track changes in Earth's surface over days, months and years. GIS is now a standard tool for environmental management, modeling and planning, and for monitoring forest cover and deforestation.

nature-es-046.title: Landscape ecology: seeing nature as a patchwork
nature-es-046.text: In 1939 the German geographer Carl Troll was studying aerial photographs, trying to see how environment and vegetation interact. He coined a name for this view from above: landscape ecology. It is the science of how ecological processes relate to particular ecosystems across whole landscapes, and how to improve those relationships. Landscapes are mixed areas of interacting patches, from forests and lakes to farms and cities. Traditional ecology often assumes places are uniform. Landscape ecology instead studies heterogeneity, the way parts of a landscape differ. Its hallmark is a focus on how pattern, process and scale relate, and on broad-scale environmental problems. Its four main principles concern how this patchiness develops, how things move across it, how it affects living and non-living processes, and how to manage it. The field treats humans explicitly as a force that reshapes landscapes and proposes ways to restore degraded ones. It grew from European planning of human-dominated landscapes and was established by 1980. Its recent growth owes much to GIS and large remotely sensed habitat datasets.

nature-es-077.title: System dynamics: why systems surprise their owners
nature-es-077.text: In the mid-1950s Jay Forrester of MIT simulated GE's hiring by hand. The firm's employment swings, he showed, came from its own structure, not the business cycle. From that insight he created system dynamics. It explains how complex systems behave over time by modeling what builds up, how fast it changes, feedback loops and time delays. Anything that builds up or runs down is a stock in this sense; its rate of change is a flow. The system's structure, its circular, interlocking and delayed relationships, often matters as much as its parts. Models update every variable in small time steps, so mutual causes play out through feedbacks and delays. Typical subjects are population, farming, ecological and economic systems, which interact strongly. The best-known model is probably {{ref:nature-eecon-154}} of 1972, which forecast economic collapse in the 21st century under many growth scenarios. Paired with GIS, system dynamics powers landscape simulations in {{ref:nature-eecon-059}}.

nature-es-063.title: Ecosystem models: simulating centuries in minutes
nature-es-063.text: No one can ethically wreck a real ecosystem to see what happens, but a model can, and it can simulate centuries in minutes. An ecosystem model is an abstract, usually mathematical, representation of an ecological system, from one population to a whole biome. Relationships measured in the field, such as sunlight and water against photosynthesis, are combined to predict how the real system behaves. Ecosystems are so complex that models reduce them to a few state variables and group similar species into functional groups. Simple analytic models are solved by equations. Simulation models are solved numerically and are more widely used and more realistic. Spatially explicit models include a varied landscape, because place can change outcomes greatly. Models are checked against independent data or field observations. The gaps often suggest new hypotheses. {{ref:nature-res-006}}, a simulation system for marine ecosystems, is widely used by fisheries scientists.

nature-es-061.title: Agent-based models: simple rules, complex worlds
nature-es-061.text: In 1971 Thomas Schelling used coins and graph paper to show how simple choices by individuals could produce segregation that none of them planned. It was an early agent-based model. Such a computer model simulates the actions and interactions of autonomous agents, such as people or organizations, to see how a whole system behaves. In ecology it is called an individual-based model. Its central ideas are agents as objects, emergence and complexity: simple rules for agents can produce complex behavior. The idea dates to the late 1940s but spread only in the 1990s, because it needs heavy computing. In economics, these models drop the assumption of equilibrium and use diverse, interdependent agents, so they can produce booms and crashes. Combined with GIS, the model captures the process while the GIS captures the spatial pattern. Water planners use them to test infrastructure and policy and to value cooperation. Calibration, sensitivity analysis and statistical tests check that a model relates to the real world.

nature-es-056.title: Land cover: what actually sits on the ground
nature-es-056.text: Between 1992 and 2015, artificial surfaces worldwide grew from 26.04 million ha to 55.40 million ha, according to FAO data. Over the same stretch, tree-covered areas fell by 99.93 million ha, to 4,335.00 million ha or 29.11% of land. These figures describe land cover: the physical material at Earth's land surface, such as plants, concrete, buildings, bare ground or water. It differs from {{ref:nature-res-107}}, which describes how people use the land and what economic activity happens there, though the two are often confused. Land cover is captured mainly by field survey or by analyzing remotely sensed images. Definitions vary: there are many definitions of forest, sometimes within one organization. Human activity is the biggest cause of land cover change, with deforestation historically a primary driver. Detecting that change gives a baseline for judging climate change impacts on habitats, biodiversity and resources.

nature-es-072.title: Scenario planning: rehearsing several futures
nature-es-072.text: In the 1970s energy companies lost billions, blindsided by environmentalism and the OPEC cartel. Royal Dutch Shell responded by adopting scenario planning, a strategic method in which organizations imagine several plausible futures to make flexible long-term plans. It presents alternative futures and the paths to them rather than one exact forecast. Unlike a forecast, it does not simply extend past trends or assume past patterns will hold. It draws on systems thinking: many factors can combine through feedback loops into surprising futures. Analysts pick scenarios that are both possible and uncomfortable, so decision-makers can anticipate change and build sturdier strategies. Most authors credit Herman Kahn, at the RAND Corporation in the 1950s, with introducing it, and Gaston Berger developed similar methods in France. In business, attention has shifted from rivals' behavior toward changes in the natural environment.

nature-es-069.title: NDVI: reading plant health from space
nature-es-069.text: Green plants look dark in red light and bright in near-infrared. They absorb visible light for photosynthesis but strongly reflect near-infrared, and that contrast is the basis of the normalized difference vegetation index. NDVI is a number, calculated from red and near-infrared sensor readings, that measures how dense and healthy vegetation is. It runs from -1 to 1. Negative values mean water or non-land, values near zero mean little vegetation, and high values mean dense, healthy plants. Dense canopies typically score about 0.3 to 0.8, while bare soils give around 0.1 to 0.2. Researchers studying Great Plains rangeland developed it to correct for the changing sun angle, and its earliest reported use was in 1973 by Rouse and colleagues. Farmers use it to assess crop health, spot stress before it is visible and predict yields. Falling NDVI can signal drought, deforestation or degraded land. It has limits: it keeps only part of the original spectral information and is affected by the atmosphere, sensors, soil and snow.

nature-es-073.title: Spatial analysis: asking where
nature-es-073.text: As far back as at least 1,400 BC, Egyptian surveyors measured taxable plots with ropes, an early root of spatial analysis. Today it is the set of formal techniques that study things through their location, shape and geographic arrangement, drawing especially on spatial statistics. In a narrower sense it is geospatial analysis, usually done with GIS software. It was developed for ecology, geology and epidemiology and now reaches forests and water, disaster risk and climate adaptation. Basic operations include stacking maps and buffering, which marks areas within a set distance of features such as roads or rivers. Gravity models estimate flows of people, materials or information between places. Its most fundamental problem is defining where the things being studied are located. Another trap is the ecological fallacy: drawing conclusions about individuals from aggregated data.

nature-es-076.title: Species distribution models: predicting where life lives
nature-es-076.text: Where will a species live when the climate shifts? Species distribution modeling uses ecological models and environmental data, most often climate, to predict where a species lives across space and time. It can project a future range under climate change, a past range, or where an invasive species might spread. Its main use is conservation: finding highly suitable habitat to prioritize sites for protection and restoration. It also helps identify climate refugia, places likely to stay suitable as the climate changes. Correlative models fit a species' observed range to environmental conditions. They are quick but describe only where the species actually lives now, and they extrapolate poorly. Mechanistic models use its physiology to work out where it could survive, handling shifting ranges better but needing much data. MaxEnt, the most widely used method, works from presence-only records even when few exist. Remote sensing and GIS have greatly expanded the data available.

nature-es-066.title: Land change models: forecasting the face of the Earth
nature-es-066.text: In 2011 a study in western Mexico ran two outwardly similar land change models and got considerably different results. That is a fair warning about a powerful tool. Land change models describe, project and explain how land cover and the human uses of land change over time. They help explain how people have changed Earth's surface and will change it, guiding decisions from a single plot to whole regions. The method applies landscape ecology and is a key part of land change science. Approaches include machine-learning models trained on past land cover, cellular models that compare neighboring areas, economic supply-and-demand models, agent-based models and hybrids. The model should fit the goal: agents for questions about policy and actors, machine learning and cellular models for spotting patterns. Practitioners use them to explore the effects of policies on water, food, urbanization and more. All carry irreducible uncertainty, and the further ahead they project, the more uncertain they become.

nature-es-058.title: Active and passive sensors
nature-es-058.text: Remote sensing instruments come in two classes. Passive sensors record energy an object reflects or emits, most often reflected sunlight; cameras, radiometers and spectrometers are common examples. Active sensors send out their own energy and measure what comes back. Radar and {{ref:nature-es-068}} are active systems that time a pulse's return to find the distance to a target.

nature-es-068.title: Lidar: measuring the world with laser light
nature-es-068.text: A 2024 lidar study found that England has 390,000 km of hedgerows. Lidar measures distance by shining a laser at a surface and timing how long the reflected light takes to return. As an active sensor, it supplies its own light and uses the speed of light to turn return time into distance. From an aircraft it can map terrain at 30-centimeter resolution or better. In forests it measures tree heights and crown widths and estimates canopy volume, biomass and carbon density.

nature-es-060.title: False-color images: seeing the invisible
nature-es-060.text: A false-color composite is an image in which wavelengths are shown in colors other than their true ones, to reveal patterns the eye cannot normally see. It is made by changing which parts of the spectrum are displayed as red, green and blue. Pseudocolor works differently: it maps a single band onto a new color scale, a trick that also works for temperature or elevation.

nature-es-052.title: Raster and vector: two ways to store a map
nature-es-052.text: Mapped things are usually treated either as discrete objects, like a house or road, or as continuous fields, like rainfall or population density. A GIS traditionally stores them in two ways: as raster images made of cells, or as vector points, lines and polygons. It can convert between them, for example by tracing lines around same-class cells of a satellite image to make vector shapes. Point clouds are a newer hybrid that pair three-dimensional points with color values.

nature-es-059.title: How sharp is a satellite's eye?
nature-es-059.text: Landsat records seven bands of light; the Hyperion sensor resolves 220, from 0.4 to 2.5 μm. That difference is spectral resolution, one of four ways to describe remote sensing data. Spatial resolution is pixel size, typically squares from 1 to 1,000 metres on a side. Radiometric resolution is how many intensity levels a sensor can tell apart, typically 8 to 14 bits, or 256 up to 16,384 shades per band. Temporal resolution is how often a satellite or plane passes over, which matters for tracking deforestation over time.

nature-es-053.title: Map overlay: stacking maps to find answers
nature-es-053.text: Map overlay combines several spatial datasets of the same area into a new one, like stacking maps of one region on top of each other. Overlays work like Venn diagrams: a union keeps everything from both inputs, while an intersect keeps only where they overlap. With rasters, overlay uses map algebra, a function that combines each layer's cell values and can weight some inputs more than others. In 1983 Dana Tomlin coined 'cartographic modeling' for producing and analyzing several thematic layers of the same area.

nature-es-055.title: Choosing the best site with GIS
nature-es-055.text: Finding the best place to restore a habitat means juggling many criteria at once. GIS multi-criteria decision analysis compares alternative places against several criteria together. Decision rules combine the criteria so the alternatives can be ranked or prioritized. The method may cut the cost and time of finding potential restoration sites.

nature-es-054.title: Spatial interpolation: filling in the gaps between samples
nature-es-054.text: Measurements taken at one place closely resemble those taken nearby. That tendency justifies spatial interpolation: building a continuous surface, usually a raster, by predicting values between measured sample points. Geostatistics, the branch of statistics for continuous spatial data, models these correlations to predict values at unmeasured places. Methods include inverse distance weighting, kriging, splines, Thiessen polygons and trend surfaces.

nature-es-062.title: Bayesian networks: reasoning backward from evidence
nature-es-062.text: A doctor sees symptoms and must work back to the likely disease. A Bayesian network does this kind of reasoning. It is a probability model that shows a set of variables and how they depend on each other, drawn as a diagram of arrows with no loops. Each node is a variable and each arrow a direct dependency. The network applies Bayes' theorem automatically, updating beliefs about unobserved variables as evidence comes in. Ecologists have used such networks to explore where ecological regime shifts are likely.

nature-es-078.title: Causal loop diagrams: drawing the feedback
nature-es-078.text: More buyers of a product mean stronger word of mouth, which brings more buyers. A causal loop diagram maps loops like that: a simple drawing of a system's parts and how they affect each other. Reinforcing loops amplify change, while counteracting loops push back. Double slashes on an arrow mark a significant delay between cause and effect. The diagram supports qualitative analysis. For numbers, it is turned into a stock and flow diagram and simulated on a computer.

nature-es-048.title: Edges and ecotones: life at the borders
nature-es-048.text: Where a forest gives way to grassland, a new kind of place appears. An ecotone is the transition zone where two ecological communities meet. It keeps traits of both neighbors and often holds species found in neither. Ecotones can be natural, like a lakeshore, or made by people, like a field cleared from forest. Fencerows, forest-to-marsh transitions and riparian zones along rivers are classic examples. An edge is the part of an ecosystem near its border, where neighboring patches make conditions differ from the interior, often changing which species live there.

nature-es-047.title: Patches, corridors and matrix: the parts of a landscape
nature-es-047.text: Landscape ecologists read land as a mosaic. A patch is a fairly uniform area that differs from its surroundings. Corridors are strips of one landscape type that differ from the land on both sides. The matrix is the well-connected background system that holds them. Connectivity measures how continuous a corridor, network or matrix is: a forest with fewer open gaps is better connected. Patches change and fluctuate over time, a process called patch dynamics.

nature-es-049.title: Fragmentation: when the landscape breaks apart
nature-es-049.text: Landscape fragmentation is the breaking up of a habitat, ecosystem or land-use type into smaller, separate pieces. Repeated random clearing, natural or human, can splinter continuous cover into isolated patches. The change is not gradual. Once cleared area passes a critical level, a landscape flips from connected to disconnected. Metapopulation models, which treat scattered groups as linked populations, gave conservation biologists a tool to judge whether populations can survive this.

nature-es-064.title: Lotka and Volterra: the dance of predator and prey
nature-es-064.text: After fishing in the Adriatic was cut back during the First World War, fish and shark numbers swung in puzzling ways. Vito Volterra built a model to explain them in 1926, a year after Alfred Lotka developed the same idea. The Lotka–Volterra model is a pair of equations, one for prey and one for its predator, describing how their numbers rise and fall together. Its parameters are the prey's growth rate, the predation rate, the predator's assimilation efficiency and the predator's death rate. It is not unchallenged: supporters of the rival Arditi–Ginzburg model argue the field data reject it.

nature-es-065.title: i-Tree: putting a value on every tree
nature-es-065.text: How much is a city's tree canopy worth? A suite of US Forest Service software called i-Tree tries to answer. It measures and values the services trees provide in cities and the countryside. It quantifies services such as pollution removal, carbon storage and rainwater runoff avoided. Some tools work up from ground inventories of trees, others down from remote sensing data. Urban foresters use it to turn a forest's structure into ecosystem services and economic value. It began in 2002 as a sample survey that simulated a full urban tree inventory.

nature-es-070.title: Participatory GIS: maps made by the people who live there
nature-es-070.text: Participatory GIS puts mapping tools in the hands of local people, so their own knowledge shapes planning decisions. It combines sketch maps, 3D models, aerial photos, satellite images and GPS to turn what people know about places into maps for discussion. Its aim is to empower marginalized groups and protect traditional knowledge by leaving control of sensitive maps with their makers. Uses range from neighborhood planning to managing forests, water and wildlife. Practitioners still debate top-down against bottom-up approaches, and critics ask who really gets access to the technology.

nature-es-080.title: InVEST: free software for mapping nature's value
nature-es-080.text: InVEST is used in more than 185 countries to map valuable ecological resources and weigh trade-offs in land and water use. The name stands for Integrated Valuation of Ecosystem Services and Trade-offs. It is free, open-source software from the Natural Capital Project for mapping and valuing ecosystem services, with 20+ models covering land, freshwater, marine, coastal and urban settings. Users steer investments toward both conservation and development. Alongside the ARIES project and the Corporate Ecosystem Services Review, it is one of several tools that help businesses value services. Its developer works with governments, banks, companies and communities to bring nature's values into decisions.

nature-es-075.title: The modifiable areal unit problem: same data, different answers
nature-es-075.text: Draw a population density map using state boundaries, then redraw it using county boundaries, and the results differ radically. This is the modifiable areal unit problem, a source of statistical bias. Results change depending on how point data are grouped into areas such as districts or regions. Totals, rates and densities all depend on both the shape and the size of the units chosen.

nature-es-074.title: Spatial autocorrelation: near things are related
nature-es-074.text: Values at nearby locations tend to be related, positively or negatively. This spatial autocorrelation breaks the independence that standard statistics assume. Regressions that ignore it can give unstable estimates and unreliable significance tests. Spatial regression models capture it, and it can also be read as useful information rather than a nuisance. Classic measures include Moran's I, Geary's C and Getis's G.

nature-es-067.title: Testing a land change model against reality
nature-es-067.text: A model can look brilliant by cheating. Calibrating it with data from after its first time period can make it seem far more accurate than it really is. Land change model validation guards against this by comparing a model's processes or predicted maps with what really happened. Pattern validation often uses three maps: the real maps at two dates and the simulated second map. Pixels are sorted into hits, misses, false alarms and similar classes. The Figure of Merit turns these into one percentage for the overlap between real and simulated change.

nature-es-071.title: Runoff curve numbers: how much rain runs off
nature-es-071.text: A paved parking lot has a curve number of 98; open space in good condition on sandy soil has 39. The runoff curve number is an empirical figure used in hydrology to predict how much rainfall runs straight off the land rather than soaking in. It ranges from 30 to 100; higher numbers mean more runoff. It depends on the soil and on how land is used and treated. Soils fall into four groups, from A, deep sands that soak water up fast, to D, clays and shallow soils that absorb it very slowly.

openers.mapping-and-modeling-services: A service cannot be protected until someone knows where it is and how it might change. This chapter is about the tools that answer those questions. Satellites and aircraft gather information about the land from a distance, and a GIS, computer hardware and software for geographic data, stores and displays it. Simple numbers calculated from sensor readings reveal how dense and healthy vegetation is, and models represent everything from one population to a whole biome. Other tools look ahead, simulating individual agents, projecting how land use and land cover will change, predicting where species will live, and imagining several plausible futures so plans can bend rather than break.

reviews.mapping-and-modeling-services: Mapping nature's services starts with seeing: satellites, lidar and NDVI turn reflected light into maps of forests, crops and hedgerows. A GIS ties those observations together by location, and spatial analysis, overlays and interpolation squeeze meaning from them, while warning of traps such as the modifiable areal unit problem. Models then ask what happens next, from Lotka and Volterra's predator and prey equations to agent-based simulations, system dynamics and land change projections whose uncertainty grows the further they look. Tools such as InVEST and i-Tree put those results into the language of value, so managers can weigh trade-offs and steer investment. None of it is certain, which is why validation and scenario planning sit beside every forecast.
